label: Canadienne

names.text: "Black Canadienne", "French Canadienne" and "Black Jersey" from the Wikipedia article's alternative-names line.

about.text: The only cattle breed originating in Canada, a small to medium-sized dairy breed from Quebec, descended from cattle from Normandy and Brittany that arrived in the 1600s. It is kept mainly for milk, which is high in butterfat and protein and suits cheese-making. Quebec gave it official heritage status in 1999.

sources.text: Wikipedia article: "the only cattle breed originating in Canada"; ancestry from cattle from Normandy and Brittany in present-day Quebec in the 1600s; "The main use of the cattle is for milk production"; "the milk contains high levels of butterfat and protein", suitable for cheese; small to medium-sized; official heritage status from the Government of Quebec in 1999.

Wikipedia article: ancestry from cattle from Normandy and Brittany that arrived in present-day Quebec in the 1600s. The breed society formed in 1895. The herd-book was established in either 1886 or 1896, depending on the source, so the range is 1886 to 1896.
Wikipedia article: "The main use of the cattle is for milk production." The article also says the cattle have been raised for beef, but that claim is tagged [citation needed], so it is left out.

Wikipedia article: "In 2025 it was listed in DAD-IS as 'at risk/endangered'", mapped to endangered. FAO (2007) is given in the same article as "endangered-maintained". The DAD-IS record itself was not opened.

facts.v: In 1999 the Government of Quebec gave the breed official heritage status.

sources.text: Wikipedia article, on the breed's heritage status.

facts.v: In 1901 the breed was recognized as the most profitable dairy breed at the Pan-American show in Buffalo, New York.

sources.text: Wikipedia article, quoting the 1901 recognition at the Pan-American show in Buffalo.

facts.v: Brown Swiss blood was introduced in the early 1970s, but the crossbreeding was stopped to preserve the breed's identity.

sources.text: Wikipedia article, on the early 1970s Brown Swiss crossing.

gaps: No current population figure found (the nearest is 2000, when the breed society had 82 members and registered 103 pure-bred cattle; registrations are not a population count, so they are not used as head). No milk yield per lactation, lactation length or fat and protein percentages found: the article gives only qualitative butterfat and protein, and the Canadian 305-day tables searched did not include a Canadienne row. The DAD-IS record itself was not opened. The herd-book date is uncertain (1886 or 1896), so the formed range covers both.
